description: Deep red plates with every crack lit orange to a hot centre. Whatever it came out of has not been brought down yet.
lore: Every other stone on a bench is in the past tense. A stone is what is left when a shape comes apart; the shape is accounted for, the creature is a matter of record, and the whole vocabulary runs that way — released, cracked, brought in. This one is sold with a tense the trade does not otherwise use. Not yet, said flatly, the way you would say a thing about scheduling.

A hundred gold, and not a fighting stone. Against anything still whole it does nothing worth the setting; against something already opened it adds twelve and hands you back a twentieth. The graders go this far and no further, and they say it as a description of the stone and of nothing else: what reached the bottom here was not hunger and was not endurance. It was a preference for things that had already begun to lose.

Then the arithmetic, which everybody does once and drops. Nineteen have come in that anyone can put a name to. [[lore/the_hard_pieces|One kind of creature, one kind of stone]] — so nineteen stones are nineteen shapes broken, by hands, at some hour, in some country, and not one of those hands has ever sat down at a fire and said so. Either it is being done quietly, which is not how crackers are; a good story is half the wage. Or the first rule anybody learns has a hole in it the exact size of this stone.
gm_notes: Unbound, and the shipped 'not yet' is honoured as the trade's own phrase rather than corrected: what the record adds is that stones exist only because shapes were broken, so nineteen of them is a count of somebody's quiet evenings. Both halves of the fork are left standing — silent crackers, or a hole in Law V — and neither is favoured. No creature is described. Description reworked because the sprite's cracks are lit, not dried.
